passage: Yesterday, Mr. Farhan stopped the whole line when I was late to assembly. “Ganga, this is the third time this week!” My face went hot and I stared at the floor. I wanted to argue that the bus had broken down, but nothing came out. Some kids thought I didn't care because I stayed silent. That wasn't true; I was ashamed. After assembly he asked me to stay behind, and this time his voice was lower. “What happened?” I told him about the bus. He said, “Then next time tell me first, and we'll fix it together.” I felt better. Being told what to do was easier than being told I was bad. Ganga.

qa.q: How many times had Ganga been late that week, according to Mr. Farhan?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Ganga stay silent and stare at the floor during the reprimand?
qa.a: Ganga was ashamed and stunned, and the silence did not mean not caring.

qa.q: What made the second talk work better than the first?
qa.a: Mr. Farhan spoke in a lower voice, asked what happened and offered to fix it together, focusing on the fix and not on shame.

qa.q: How might the classmates have seen Ganga's silence?
qa.a: They may have thought Ganga did not care, though that was not true.

grounding: A child receiving a reprimand goes silent and looks down, which does not prove indifference, and the adult focuses on the behaviour and the fix.

passage: Teacher's note. Nilesh's homework was missing again, and I said in front of the class, “This is not acceptable.” Nilesh looked down, said nothing and then began to argue in a low voice that he had done it. I said the matter would be settled after class. Afterwards he cried quietly and told me his little brother had torn the pages. I realised my reprimand had been about the pages and not about the effort. I asked him to redo the work by Friday, and told him he could bring it to me if it went wrong again. Nilesh nodded and wiped his face. I should have asked before speaking. Ms. Gurleen.

qa.q: Who tore Nilesh's homework pages?
qa.a: His little brother.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's downcast look and low arguing suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggested he felt ashamed and unfairly judged, which the teacher later understood after hearing about the torn pages.

qa.q: What would the teacher do differently next time?
qa.a: She would ask what happened before reprimanding him in front of the class, focusing on the behaviour and the fix.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's classmates have felt watching the reprimand?
qa.a: Some may have felt sorry for him, others uneasy, and they may have wondered whether they would be next.

grounding: A child who is reprimanded looks down, argues and cries, and the reaction does not prove guilt, so the adult should ask first and focus on the fix.

passage: Tuesday. Jasleen's diary. Today Ma'am told Gurpreet off for not bringing her project, again. Gurpreet didn't look down like most people. She argued. “It's not my fault! You don't know anything!” The whole class went silent. I thought, She's so rude, she doesn't even care. Ma'am didn't shout back. She said, “Let's talk about getting it done, not about fault. When can you bring it?” Gurpreet's chin wobbled. “Friday. My Nani's in hospital, and we've been there every night.” Ma'am's voice went soft. “Friday is fine. Thank you for telling me.” I felt bad for thinking she didn't care. Arguing was just how the worry came out.

qa.q: Why had Gurpreet's family been at the hospital every night?
qa.a: Gurpreet's Nani was in hospital.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when she argued back?
qa.a: Gurpreet was worried and stressed about her Nani in hospital, and it came out as defensive arguing.

qa.q: How did Ma'am handle the reprimand well?
qa.a: She didn't shout back or shame Gurpreet; she focused on when the project could be done, which let the real reason come out.

qa.q: How did Jasleen first read Gurpreet's arguing?
qa.a: Jasleen first read it as rudeness and not caring, then felt bad on learning the worry behind it.

grounding: Shows a child arguing back when reprimanded, a reaction that did not mean indifference, and an adult focusing on the fix rather than shame.

passage: The goats had eaten half the okra plants by the time Madhuri came out of the house. “Avni! You left the gate open again!” Avni stood by the broken fence, eyes on the ground, saying nothing. Her silence made Madhuri crosser. “Don't you care? Say something!” Avni's lips pressed tight, but still nothing came. Madhuri stopped. She remembered her own father's shouting, and how she had gone silent too, not because she didn't care, but because the words wouldn't come. She took a breath. “Okay. The plants are gone. Let's fix the gate so it closes by itself.” Together they tied a stone to a rope as a weight. Avni finally whispered, “Sorry, Amma.”

qa.q: What did the goats eat?
qa.a: The goats ate half the okra plants.

qa.q: What was Avni likely feeling as she stood silent?
qa.a: Avni was likely ashamed and upset, too overwhelmed to find words, not uncaring.

qa.q: What did Madhuri change that helped?
qa.a: She stopped demanding words and focused on the fix, weighting the gate together, which let Avni say sorry.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri recognise Avni's silence?
qa.a: Madhuri remembered going silent under her own father's shouting, not because she didn't care but because the words wouldn't come.

grounding: Shows a child going silent when reprimanded, which does not prove indifference, and a parent turning to the fix instead of shame.

passage: In the Copenhagen classroom, Ms Ingrid Holm asked Yuki, for the third time, to stop whispering during the test instructions. “Yuki, that's enough. Move to the front desk, please.” Yuki's face crumpled, and tears ran down before she could stop them. Someone at the back muttered, “So dramatic.” Ms Holm heard. She didn't let the tears change the rule, and she didn't make a bigger fuss either. After the test she crouched by Yuki's desk. “Moving you wasn't a punishment for being bad. It was so you could hear. What were you whispering about?” Yuki sniffed. “I didn't understand the instructions. I was asking Leo.” Ms Holm nodded. “Next time, ask me.”

qa.q: Where did Ms Holm ask Yuki to move?
qa.a: She asked Yuki to move to the front desk.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when she cried?
qa.a: Yuki felt embarrassed and upset at being told off in front of everyone, when she had only been asking for help.

qa.q: How did Ms Holm handle the tears and the rule?
qa.a: She kept the rule but didn't shame Yuki, then privately explained the move and found out the real reason for the whispering.

qa.q: How did the student at the back read Yuki's tears?
qa.a: They read the tears as being dramatic, not knowing Yuki was confused and embarrassed.

grounding: Shows a child crying when reprimanded, which does not prove guilt, and a teacher focusing on the behaviour and the fix.

passage: The library bell had already rung when Mrs Qureshi found the atlas with its map page torn along the fold. Hafsa was the last one who had borrowed it. "Hafsa, this page was fine last week," Mrs Qureshi said. Hafsa stared at her sandals and said nothing. Her ears went pink. Two boys behind the shelf whispered, "See, she did it." Mrs Qureshi knew silence can mean fear as easily as guilt. She crouched and lowered her voice. "I'm not here to scold you. I just need to know what happened to the page, and then we can mend it." Hafsa's chin wobbled. "It was already loose. I tried to hold it and it ripped more." Mrs Qureshi fetched the clear tape, and they fixed the map together.

qa.q: What did Mrs Qureshi fetch at the end?
qa.a: She fetched the clear tape, and they fixed the map together.

qa.q: What might Hafsa's silence and pink ears suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely she felt scared and embarrassed at being questioned with others listening. The silence did not prove guilt: she later explained the page was already loose.

qa.q: Which choice helped Hafsa speak up, and why?
qa.a: Mrs Qureshi crouched, lowered her voice and said she only needed to know what happened so they could mend it. Taking the shame out made it safe for Hafsa to explain.

qa.q: How did the whispering boys read the silence differently from Mrs Qureshi?
qa.a: The boys took Hafsa's silence as proof that she did it, while Mrs Qureshi knew it might just be fear, so she asked instead of deciding.

grounding: It shows a child's silent, downcast reaction to a reprimand being read as possible fear rather than proof of guilt, and an adult turning to the fix instead of shame.
